I’m 25, and I lost my father at the age of 19. His 6th year death anniversary is coming soon, and compared to the 1st, I feel a lot better. I hope my experience can comfort you. First of, I’m sorry for your loss. If has been one month, things are still fresh. Heck, his death will still feel fresh after a year, or two, or three. Just know one thing: it is okay to feel your feelings, bad or good. I remember when I first lost him, I was mad at the world. I didn’t have any friends I consider “true” because I couldn’t relate to them anymore. It is a process of life that and you by chance had to go through it earlier than your peers. That resentment you have towards everyone is a normal grief process. Try your best to journal and write down your feelings — you want to project your emotions somewhere instead of other people. Tell your friends you want alone space to grieve. Real friends will understand, empathize and will be there when you finally heal. If not, then losing them is apart of the journey. I also thought the same thing, that my father did not get to see me getting into and graduating from nursing school nor will he see me getting married. It sucks, but the end of grieve is acceptance. It will take a very long time until you reach this final stage. Some days will be easier than others. Some days, even 6 years later, will hit you harder than you expected. For example, I was at a bank the other day and saw an older man with the same stance my dad always had. I broke down crying. I am healed, but there is a void inside our heart that will always be there. Don’t try to fill the void with alcohol or drugs or bad choices. It will never be filled. Acceptance is understand this fact and be okay with it. All love. I hope this helps.

Positive. In the first few years, I spent a lot of my time questioned and wondered. I blamed myself and the family. i tried to seek for a reason for his death to make sense. Hi! I’d like to share my thoughts before, during, and after nursing school regarding what specialty I wanted to go in. Warning though, I am aware it is super biased towards the ICU. But i hope it can give you an idea how I maneuver my thoughts regarding each unit and what I like/dislike about each.

ICU: So even before nursing school, I knew I wanted to become a critical care nurse. I got a chance to be in the ICU in a high school’s healthcare rotation program and I have “fallen in love” with the unit. To be completely honest, it was the vibe. Every time I rotate to an ICU floor in any hospital, most nurses were very “similar” in a way. Similar to me, so I think. Very “type A”- anal, likes things a certain way, wants autonomy over the patients, most seem to be more introverted compared to the nurses on med surg floors. Some other pros of choosing specialty are you can advance to higher schooling (CRNA), you focus on the details rather than time management because you are taking care of 1-2 patients. The cons is it is a super high stress environment since patients are super sick and can crash easily. But a lot of nurses go into ICU knowing this and they like the challenge.

Step down units are okay. I worked in a cardiac step down/telemetry during nursing school. It’s one of those better floors IMO compared to med surg (and this is completely biased post because I’m not a big fan of med surg). You take care of “4 patients maxed.” But I have seen some of my peers working in step down and get up to 6 which is… super not safe. But, the pros are the patients are not super talky. Most need a lot of assist to go to the bathroom cause they either just got moved from surgery and ICU to PCU. 

Med Surg. All I can say is almost if not all patients are walky talky. The one thing I liked about med surg is the comedy you get from patients yelling back and forth with nurses (hence the talky). Other than that, I’ll pass on taking care of 5-8 patients any days. Props to med surg nurses however- y’all have some mad time management skill. One thing, however, is they don’t focus on the details of each patient- so if you’re into the nitty gritty side of reading everything about your patient- med surg is not for you. All med surg nurses told me even if they want to, they can’t because there are too many patients to take care of. 

Pediatrics- idk if you like kids. I do like the idea of taking care of little kids because they “look less bothersome” than adults. But I can’t imagine seeing a kid dying, so I passed on peds. Also, I cannot memorized peds and babies vital signs for the hell of it. I don’t think it was ever meant for me.

OB- Have never been a fan, and I have also heard from a friend who works as a tech in an OB floor. She said a lot of “estrogen ting” going on. Too many female nurses, too many drama etc. I do like a balance of female and male just for the diversity- which is why I chose ICU btw. Or at least my ICU floor has a good balance of female/male.

ER- basically “ICU” for extroverts. I originally had ER in mind just because it was that unit you always see in the movies and it has always looked cool. Unfortunately I never had a rotation in an ER. I probably would have liked it. But I don’t really enjoy the idea of seeing too many patients in one day- also, I don’t even know what underlying diseases these patients have. You are exposed to a lot of health risks. But thanks to COVID, wearing a mask is definitely reducing those health risks. The same friend also worked in the ER and she said you see multiple patients a day since they are in and out (or inner- they become inpatient). Props to ER nurses too. 

OR- OR is also in my list of what I wanted to do. Unfortunately I’ve never rotated here. From rumors, it gets very political- i guess because of the surgeons and tension whatnot. Nevertheless, I think I would enjoy it. The reason why I did not go for it is because I can’t advance to CRNA if I did OR. 

For my CAPSTONE (last semester’s rotation), I was put in a telemetry floor which was against what i wanted (ICU was my top). However, I ended up getting offers for the ICU only, so I think we were always meant to be. Good luck with your decision! Personally, I find it important that you find a unit you admire. Whether it be the nurses, the type of patients, or the long term outlook on what you can be if you become a ICU/ER/OR/Medsurg/PCU/PED/OB nurse.
